prompt: What structural feature characterizes an organic acid?

choices.text: A positively polarized hydrogen atom
An atom with a lone pair of electrons that can bond to H^+
choices.why: That is the mark of an organic base, such as methylamine.

choices.text: A negatively charged carbon atom
choices.why: Organic acids are neutral molecules; what they need is a δ+ hydrogen they can lose as H^+.

choices.text: Any C–H bond
choices.why: Most C–H bonds are not acidic. A C–H hydrogen is acidic only when the carbon is next to a C=O bond, as in acetone.

explanation: Organic acids are characterized by a positively polarized hydrogen atom (blue in electrostatic potential maps), which can be lost as H^+.

prompt: Which pair describes the two main kinds of organic acid?

choices.text: Those with an O–H bond, and those with a C–H next to a C=O bond (O=C–C–H)
Those with an O–H bond, and those with an N–H bond
choices.why: Nitrogen compounds such as methylamine are the most common organic bases, not one of the two main kinds of acid.

choices.text: Those with a C=O bond, and those with a C=C bond
choices.why: A double bond alone doesn't make an acid; there must be a positively polarized hydrogen to lose.

choices.text: Those with a C–H bond on any carbon, and those with an O–H bond
choices.why: Only a C–H next to a C=O bond is acidic, because its conjugate base is resonance-stabilized.

explanation: Organic acids are of two main kinds: acids such as methanol and acetic acid, with a hydrogen bonded to an electronegative oxygen (O–H), and acids such as acetone, with a hydrogen bonded to a carbon next to a C=O bond (O=C–C–H).

prompt: What is the pKa of acetic acid?
explanation: Acetic acid has pKa 4.76, which makes it a stronger acid than methanol (15.54) or acetone (19.3).

prompt: What is the pKa of methanol, CH3OH?
explanation: Methanol has pKa 15.54. It contains an O–H bond and is a weak acid, weaker than acetic acid (4.76).

prompt: What is the pKa of acetone, CH3COCH3?
explanation: Acetone has pKa 19.3. Its acidic hydrogens are on carbons next to the C=O bond, and it is a weaker acid than methanol (15.54) or acetic acid (4.76).

prompt: Which list puts methanol, acetic acid, and acetone in order from strongest to weakest acid?

choices.text: Acetic acid > methanol > acetone
Acetone > methanol > acetic acid
choices.why: That is weakest to strongest. The lower the pKa, the stronger the acid: 4.76 < 15.54 < 19.3.

choices.text: Methanol > acetic acid > acetone
choices.why: Both have O–H bonds, but acetic acid is stronger because its conjugate base is also resonance-stabilized.

choices.text: Acetic acid > acetone > methanol
choices.why: Acetone (pKa 19.3) is weaker than methanol (pKa 15.54); its acidic hydrogen is on carbon, not oxygen.

explanation: The pKa values are 4.76 for acetic acid, 15.54 for methanol, and 19.3 for acetone. Methanol is a weak acid, acetic acid a somewhat stronger one, and acetone weaker still.

prompt: Why is methanol, CH3OH, acidic at all?

choices.text: Its conjugate base has the negative charge on a strongly electronegative oxygen atom
Its conjugate base is stabilized by resonance
choices.why: Methoxide, CH3O^−, has no resonance forms. Resonance is the extra stabilization that makes acetic acid stronger.

choices.text: Its C–H hydrogens are next to a C=O bond
choices.why: Methanol has no C=O bond. Its acidic hydrogen is the one on oxygen.

choices.text: Oxygen's lone pairs can accept H^+
choices.why: Accepting H^+ is what methanol does when it acts as a base, not as an acid.

explanation: Methanol contains an O–H bond. Its acidity is due to the fact that the conjugate base formed by loss of H^+ (methoxide ion) is stabilized by having its negative charge on a strongly electronegative oxygen atom.

prompt: Methanol and acetic acid both lose H^+ from an O–H bond. Why is acetic acid the stronger acid?

choices.text: Its conjugate base, acetate, is also stabilized by resonance
Its O–H hydrogen is on a more electronegative atom
choices.why: In both acids the hydrogen is on oxygen. The difference is that acetate's charge is spread by resonance.

choices.text: It has more hydrogen atoms to lose
choices.why: The number of hydrogens doesn't set acid strength; the stability of the conjugate base does.

choices.text: Its conjugate base has no negative charge
choices.why: Acetate carries a negative charge, but it is shared between two oxygens by resonance.

explanation: In both cases the conjugate base has its negative charge on an electronegative oxygen. In addition, the conjugate base of acetic acid is stabilized by resonance (Sections 2.4 and 2.5), which makes acetic acid the stronger acid.

prompt: Why is acetone acidic even though its acidic hydrogen is bonded to carbon?

choices.text: Its conjugate base is resonance-stabilized, and one resonance form puts the negative charge on oxygen
Carbon is more electronegative than oxygen
choices.why: Oxygen is the more electronegative atom; that's why the resonance form with the charge on oxygen helps.

choices.text: Its C–H bonds are polarized with hydrogen δ−
choices.why: An acidic hydrogen is positively polarized (δ+), not negatively.

choices.text: Acetone loses H^+ from its oxygen atom
choices.why: Acetone's oxygen carries no hydrogen. The H^+ comes from a carbon next to the C=O.

explanation: The acidity of acetone and other compounds with C=O bonds is due to resonance stabilization of the conjugate base formed by loss of H^+. In addition, one of the resonance forms stabilizes the negative charge by placing it on an electronegative oxygen atom.

prompt: In what form do carboxylic acids usually exist at the typical pH of 7.3 inside cells?

choices.text: Dissociated, as carboxylate anions, –CO2^−
Undissociated, as –CO2H
choices.why: At pH 7.3 carboxylic acids have usually lost their acidic hydrogen.

choices.text: Protonated, as positively charged ions
choices.why: At cellular pH a carboxylic acid loses H^+; it doesn't gain one.

choices.text: As zwitterions
choices.why: Zwitterions form when one molecule has both an acidic and a basic site, as in amino acids.

explanation: Carboxylic acids contain the –CO2H group. At the typical pH of 7.3 found within cells, they are usually dissociated and exist as their carboxylate anions, –CO2^−.

prompt: What structural feature characterizes an organic base?

choices.text: An atom with a lone pair of electrons that can bond to H^+
A positively polarized hydrogen atom
choices.why: That characterizes an organic acid.

choices.text: A hydroxide ion, OH^−
choices.why: Organic bases are usually neutral molecules such as methylamine; what they need is a lone pair.

choices.text: A vacant orbital
choices.why: A vacant orbital lets a substance accept an electron pair, which is what an acid does.

explanation: Organic bases are characterized by an atom (reddish in electrostatic potential maps) with a lone pair of electrons that can bond to H^+.

prompt: Which compounds are the most common organic bases?

choices.text: Nitrogen-containing compounds such as methylamine
Oxygen-containing compounds such as methanol
choices.why: Oxygen compounds can act as bases, but only toward a sufficiently strong acid; nitrogen compounds are the most common bases.

choices.text: Carboxylic acids such as acetic acid
choices.why: Carboxylic acids are best known as acids; at cellular pH they exist as carboxylate anions.

choices.text: Hydrocarbons such as pentane
choices.why: A base needs a lone pair to bond to H^+; hydrocarbons have none.

explanation: Nitrogen-containing compounds such as methylamine are the most common organic bases and are involved in almost all metabolic pathways. Oxygen-containing compounds can also act as bases when reacting with a sufficiently strong acid.

prompt: When does methanol, CH3OH, act as a base?

choices.text: When its oxygen atom accepts a proton from a sufficiently strong acid
When it donates the proton on its oxygen
choices.why: Donating a proton is what methanol does when it acts as an acid.

choices.text: Never; methanol is only an acid
choices.why: Like water, methanol can act as either an acid or a base depending on the circumstances.

choices.text: When its carbon atom accepts a proton
choices.why: The base site is an atom with a lone pair; in methanol that is the oxygen.

explanation: Some oxygen-containing compounds can act as both acids and bases, just as water can. Methanol and acetone act as acids when they donate a proton, but as bases when their oxygen atom accepts a proton.

prompt: Why are amino acids so named?

choices.text: They are both amines (–NH2) and carboxylic acids (–CO2H)
They are acids that contain ammonia, NH3, as a separate molecule
choices.why: The amine is part of the same molecule as the –CO2H group.

choices.text: They are acids formed only by the breakdown of proteins
choices.why: The name comes from their two functional groups: an amine and a carboxylic acid.

choices.text: They contain an O–H bond next to a C=O, like acetone
choices.why: Acetone has a C–H next to a C=O. Amino acids are named for their –NH2 and –CO2H groups.

explanation: Amino acids are so named because they are both amines (–NH2) and carboxylic acids (–CO2H). They are the building blocks of the proteins in all living organisms.

prompt: How many different amino acids go into making up proteins?
explanation: Twenty different amino acids go into making up proteins; alanine is an example.

prompt: Why does alanine exist mainly as a zwitterion rather than in its uncharged form?

choices.text: It has acidic and basic sites in the same molecule, so it undergoes an internal acid–base reaction
It loses an electron to form a cation
choices.why: A zwitterion is doubly charged, with both a positive and a negative site, and forms by proton transfer.

choices.text: It reacts with a second alanine molecule
choices.why: The acid–base reaction is internal: the –CO2H and –NH2 groups of the same molecule react.

choices.text: It has no acidic hydrogens, only basic sites
choices.why: Alanine has both: an acidic –CO2H group and a basic –NH2 group.

explanation: Alanine and other amino acids exist primarily in a doubly charged form called a zwitterion. It arises because amino acids have both acidic and basic sites within the same molecule and therefore undergo an internal acid–base reaction.
